title: Layer 7 — Application
summary: The OSI layer where applications meet the network: HTTP, DNS, SMTP, SSH, and the data they exchange.
what: Layer 7 is where the message has meaning to a program: a GET, a DNS question, an SMTP MAIL FROM. Protocols here specify verbs, headers, and payloads. The OSI 'application' is not the GUI — it is the protocol the process speaks.
why: When users say 'the website is down', the first skilled question is whether DNS, TLS, TCP, or HTTP is the part that failed. That is an L7-vs-below split.
mental: The letter’s words. Lower layers deliver bytes; this layer parses them as a request.
points: Purpose: application-level messages and the protocols that define them.
PDU: data (messages). Addressing: URLs, hostnames, service names — not ports (those are L4).
Protocols: HTTP/HTTPS, DNS, SMTP, FTP, SSH, DHCP, WebSockets (upgrade).
Devices: end hosts, L7 load balancers and API gateways, reverse proxies.
Example: GET /index.html, Host: example.com.

interview.a: Yes in OSI teaching. In TCP/IP it sits in the application layer on top of TCP (or QUIC).

interview.q: Does a URL include a layer-4 idea?
interview.a: The host is resolved by DNS (L7); the port is L4. The path is application.

title: Layer 6 — Presentation
summary: Syntax and encryption in the OSI teaching model: encodings, compression, and (often) TLS.
what: Layer 6 is the translation layer in the OSI picture: character encodings, serialization, compression, and encryption so layer 7 can speak a canonical form. On the internet this work is folded into the application (TLS, JSON, gzip, protobuf).
why: Interviewers still place TLS here. Real RFCs place TLS above TCP. Knowing both sentences is the adult answer.
mental: Agreeing on a language and whether the envelope is opaque (encrypted) before the post office sees it.
points: Purpose: make data understandable and, often, confidential/integrity-protected.
PDU: still 'data'. No extra addressing.
Examples: UTF-8, JPEG, TLS records, ASN.1, gzip.
Devices: hosts. Middleboxes that terminate TLS pretend to be the presentation layer.
mistakes: Saying 'TLS is layer 6' as if the kernel had an L6 module

interview.a: Teaching OSI: presentation. TCP/IP: application, over TCP. QUIC: crypto is in the transport.
Encoding (UTF-8 vs UTF-16) and encryption (TLS). Compression is the third textbook one.

extra.title: TLS is not cleanly L6
extra.text: TLS is specified as an application protocol over a reliable stream (TCP) or as part of QUIC. OSI L6 is a teaching bucket for 'syntax + crypto', not a Linux subsystem.

title: Layer 5 — Session
summary: Dialogs: setup, teardown, and checkpoints. Thin on the internet; explicit in some RPC systems.
what: Layer 5 in OSI manages a conversation: establish, checkpoint, recover, tear down. TCP already gives a byte-stream session; HTTP/2 streams and TLS sessions absorbed more. RPC systems (and NetBIOS) made this layer visible.
why: It is the layer people fail to name in interviews, and the right answer is: the function exists, the internet did not keep it as a separate protocol suite.
mental: The phone call, not the words and not the copper: who is talking to whom, and can we resume.
points: Purpose: organize a dialog between two presentation entities.
PDU: data, sometimes with a session id.
Examples: RPC conversations, SMB sessions, TLS session resumption as a cousin.
On TCP/IP this is folded into TCP + the application.
mistakes: Inventing a session protocol that TCP already is

interview.q: Why does L5 feel empty on the internet?
interview.a: TCP’s connection is already a session. Applications added their own (HTTP/2 streams, TLS sessions).

title: Layer 4 — Transport
summary: Process-to-process: ports, reliability, and congestion control. TCP and UDP live here.
what: Layer 4 delivers data between two processes (sockets). It adds ports so many conversations share one host. TCP adds a connection, reliability, order, flow control, and congestion control. UDP adds ports and a checksum, then stops.
why: Almost every interview that starts at HTTP walks down to TCP. Ports, the handshake, and 'TCP vs UDP' are the core.
mental: The courier who knows which apartment (port) in the building (host) should get the package, and whether you wanted a signature (TCP) or just a toss (UDP).
points: Purpose: end-to-end process communication.
PDU: TCP segment or UDP datagram. Addressing: 16-bit ports.
Protocols: TCP, UDP, SCTP, QUIC (which also eats some of TLS and HTTP/3).
Devices: end hosts; L4 load balancers NAT on the 4-tuple.
Reliability, ordering, flow control, congestion control — TCP yes, UDP no.
mistakes: Thinking TCP 'guarantees delivery' if the peer is gone
Using UDP and forgetting you now own retransmission

interview.a: Source IP, dest IP, source port, dest port. That is a TCP connection.

interview.q: TCP vs UDP in two contrasts.
interview.a: Connection + reliability vs datagrams + no retransmission. Ports exist on both.

title: Layer 3 — Network
summary: Host-to-host across hops: IP, routing, ICMP. Packets and logical addresses.
what: Layer 3 moves packets from a source IP to a destination IP across many L2 hops. Routers look at the destination, match the longest prefix, decrement TTL, and wrap a new L2 frame for the next hop. ICMP is the error and diagnostic plane.
why: This is why the internet scales: hierarchical addresses and hop-by-hop forwarding. Subnetting, NAT, and traceroute all live here.
mental: The city name on the envelope. Each post office (router) only needs to know the next city, not the whole path.
points: Purpose: logical addressing and routing across networks.
PDU: packet. Addressing: IPv4 (32-bit) / IPv6 (128-bit).
Protocols: IPv4, IPv6, ICMP, OSPF, BGP (routing protocols are L3 control).
Devices: routers. Hosts have L3 too (their own stack).
TTL/hop limit stops loops. Fragmentation is IPv4’s historical mess; IPv6 avoids it in the path.
mistakes: Saying a router 'strips TCP' — it usually only rewrites L2 and looks at L3

interview.q: What does a router change on a packet?
interview.a: L2 encapsulation (new MACs), TTL, sometimes checksum. Source/dest IP usually stay (unless NAT).
Among routes that cover the dest, pick the most specific (longest mask). Default is /0.

title: Layer 2 — Data Link
summary: Hop-to-hop frames: MAC addresses, Ethernet, switches, and error detection.
what: Layer 2 moves a frame between two NICs on a single link or LAN. Ethernet headers carry MACs and an EtherType (0x0800 for IPv4). Switches learn source MACs and forward/flood. CRC detects corruption on the wire.
why: ARP, VLANs, switching loops, and 'link light up but no ping' are L2 problems. You cannot debug a LAN without this layer.
mental: The truck between two adjacent post offices. The city name (IP) stays in the letter; the truck only cares about the next dock (MAC).
points: Purpose: hop-to-hop transfer, framing, media access, error detection.
PDU: frame. Addressing: MAC (48-bit typical).
Protocols: Ethernet, Wi-Fi (802.11), PPP, ARP (a glue protocol).
Devices: switches, bridges, APs, NICs. Hubs are L1.
Switches split collision domains; VLANs split broadcast domains.
mistakes: Thinking a MAC is globally how the internet routes (it is not)

interview.a: Switch: L2, MAC, one broadcast domain (unless VLANs). Router: L3, IP, between subnets.
Resolve IPv4 → MAC on a LAN so the frame can be addressed.

title: Layer 1 — Physical
summary: Bits on a medium: voltage, light, radio, connectors, and Shannon’s limits.
what: Layer 1 is the analog (or optical) world: how a bit is a voltage, a light pulse, or a radio symbol. Cables, connectors, repeaters, hubs, NICs’ PHYs. No addresses, no frames — just a stream of symbols and a link that is up or down.
why: If the link light is off, nothing above exists. Bandwidth, latency (propagation), and BER start here.
mental: The road. No road, no trucks, no letters.
points: Purpose: transmit raw bits over a medium.
PDU: bits / symbols. No addressing.
Media: twisted pair, coax, fiber, radio. Encoding and modulation.
Devices: hubs, repeaters, transceivers, cables, the PHY side of a NIC.
Limits: Shannon capacity, attenuation, noise, duplex vs half-duplex.
mistakes: Confusing bandwidth (Hz or bps) with throughput

interview.a: Hub: L1 repeater, one collision domain. Switch: L2, per-port collision domain.
Propagation, transmission, queueing, processing. L1 is mostly the first two.

title: TCP/IP Model
summary: Four layers the internet actually runs: application, transport, internet, network access.
what: The DoD / Internet model has four layers: Application (OSI 7–5), Transport (OSI 4), Internet (OSI 3), Network Access / Link (OSI 2–1). IP sits in the internet layer; TCP/UDP in transport; HTTP/DNS in application. This is what RFCs and kernels implement.
why: OSI is the vocabulary; TCP/IP is the running system. You need both: one to talk, one to read code and packet captures.
mental: The same sandwich, cut into four layers instead of seven. Presentation and session are eaten by the application.
points: Application: HTTP, DNS, SSH, TLS…
Transport: TCP, UDP, QUIC.
Internet: IP, ICMP, routing.
Link: Ethernet, Wi-Fi, ARP, PPP, the PHY.
Encapsulation: data → segment → packet → frame → bits. Same story as OSI.
mistakes: Treating the two models as competing religions
Forgetting that 'link' includes both MAC and PHY

interview.q: Which model does the internet run?
interview.a: TCP/IP. OSI is the teaching and troubleshooting vocabulary.

title: OSI vs TCP/IP
summary: A seven-layer teaching model versus a four-layer running model. Same ideas, different cuts.
what: OSI (ISO/IEC 7498) specified a full protocol suite that lost. Its seven-layer map survived as a language. TCP/IP won as the implementation. The functions (addressing, hops, processes, syntax, applications) exist in both; they are grouped differently.
why: Exam questions love the mapping. Real work loves knowing that TLS is not a kernel 'presentation module' and that a multilayer switch blurs L2/L3 on purpose.
mental: Two ways to slice the same stack of wrappers around an HTTP body.
points: OSI: 7 layers, strict service definitions, a failed protocol suite.
TCP/IP: 4 layers, messy, deployed.
L5/L6 in OSI are real jobs (sessions, encodings, crypto) done inside apps on the internet.
Troubleshooting still uses OSI names: 'is this L1 or L3?'
mistakes: Saying OSI is deprecated so you can skip layer names
Mapping QUIC to a single OSI layer — it straddles

interview.q: Name a protocol that punches holes in strict layering.
